drills.q: A sensor randomly drops readings due to transient hardware noise unrelated to the true value. What missingness mechanism is this, and is drop/mean-impute valid?
drills.a: MCAR. Both dropping rows and mean-imputing are unbiased under MCAR, though still lossy -- you throw away information even if you don't introduce bias.

drills.q: You mean-impute a column with 30% missing values. The imputed column's correlation with the target drops sharply compared to what it was in the observed-only subset. What happened?
drills.a: Mean imputation collapsed variance -- every imputed value is identical, so those rows contribute zero variance and dilute whatever real correlation existed in the observed rows proportionally to the missingness rate.

drills.q: Income is missing far more often for self-employed respondents than salaried ones, and employment_type is fully observed. Which mechanism, and what's the valid fix?
drills.a: MAR -- missingness depends on an observed variable (employment_type), not the missing income value itself. Fix: model-based imputation (KNN or MICE) that conditions on employment_type and other observed columns, not a flat mean.

drills.q: A feature is 0% missing throughout training but starts showing 5% missing values in production three weeks after deploy. The XGBoost model's predictions on those rows look wrong. Diagnose.
drills.a: XGBoost never learned a split direction for that feature's missingness because it never saw a missing value during training, so it falls back to a fixed default direction (documented as right branch) that may be arbitrarily wrong for this feature. Fix: monitor per-feature missingness rate in production and retrain/explicitly impute once a previously-complete feature starts showing nulls.

drills.q: df.describe() on an 'age' column shows a minimum of -999 next to a 25th percentile of 24, with -999 appearing exactly 340 times. Is this an outlier or something else, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: A sentinel value, not a real outlier or missing value -- a real outlier wouldn't repeat the exact same number 340 times. Recode -999 to NaN explicitly, then run it through the normal MCAR/MAR/MNAR diagnosis rather than leaving it as a numeric value that wrecks the mean and any distance-based method.

drills.q: You're building a credit scoring pipeline with both a logistic regression and an XGBoost model. Design the missing-data handling for each.
drills.a: XGBoost: no explicit imputation, rely on native missing-value handling, but monitor per-feature missingness rate so a newly-missing feature doesn't silently hit an unlearned fallback. Logistic regression: fit MICE or KNN imputation on training data only, freeze the fitted imputer, apply identically at serving -- never refit live on serving data. For any column where missingness correlates with an observed field, add a was_missing flag to both models.

drills.q: A regulator asks why you imputed missing income instead of dropping those rows in a credit model. Justify your choice.
drills.a: Dropping is only defensible under MCAR. Income missingness in a credit context is plausibly MAR (correlated with employment type) or MNAR (high earners under-reporting) -- dropping those rows would systematically bias the training population away from exactly the applicants the model needs to score correctly, a fair-lending concern as well as a statistical one.

drills.q: Your train/test split shows an unrealistically small generalization gap. You suspect duplicate rows from a retried ingestion. Why is df.duplicated() insufficient, and what do you check instead?
drills.a: df.duplicated() only catches exact row equality and misses near-duplicates from truncation, floating-point differences, or slightly different timestamps on a re-ingested retry. Check for a true business key (transaction ID or hash of immutable fields) and look for test-set rows that are near-duplicates of training rows by that key.

drills.q: A categorical column has 3x the cardinality domain knowledge suggests it should. What are the two most likely corrupt-data causes, and how do you distinguish them?
drills.a: Encoding mojibake (wrong charset on read, garbling non-ASCII characters into extra fake categories) or silent truncation (a length limit cutting off values, creating near-duplicate prefix categories). Distinguish by checking whether extra categories are byte-garbled versions of real ones (mojibake) or clean prefixes of longer existing categories (truncation).

drills.q: Explain why MNAR data can't be fixed by any imputation method that only uses observed data.
drills.a: By definition, missingness under MNAR depends on the missing value itself (e.g. high earners refusing to report income) -- imputing from observed data alone at best recovers a conditional mean given what you CAN observe, which is a biased estimate of the true missing value precisely because the value's own magnitude drove the missingness. The honest fix is a was_missing flag plus explicit documentation that the feature is unreliable for that subpopulation, not a cleverer imputer.
